title: Influence of Topic Familiarity and Prompt Specificity on Citation Fabrication in Mental Health Research Using Large Language Models: Experimental Study
abstract: Background Mental health researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to improve efficiency, yet these tools can generate fabricated but plausible-sounding content (hallucinations). A notable form of hallucination involves fabricated bibliographic citations that cannot be traced to real publications. Although previous studies have explored citation fabrication across disciplines, it remains unclear whether citation accuracy in LLM output systematically varies across topics within the same field that differ in public visibility, scientific maturity, and specialization. Objective This study aims to examine the frequency and nature of citation fabrication and bibliographic errors in GPT-4o (Omni) outputs when generating literature reviews on mental health topics that varied in public familiarity and scientific maturity. We also tested whether prompt specificity (general vs specialized) influenced fabrication or accuracy rates. Methods In June 2025, GPT-4o was prompted to generate 6 literature reviews (~2000 words; ≥20 citations) on 3 disorders representing different levels of public awareness and research coverage: major depressive disorder (high), binge eating disorder (moderate), and body dysmorphic disorder (low). Each disorder was reviewed at 2 levels of specificity: a general overview (symptoms, impacts, and treatments) and a specialized review (evidence for digital interventions). All citations were extracted (N=176) and systematically verified using Google Scholar, Scopus, PubMed, WorldCat, and publisher databases. Citations were classified as fabricated (no identifiable source), real with errors, or fully accurate. Fabrication and accuracy rates were compared by disorder and review type by using chi-square tests. Results Across the 6 reviews, GPT-4o generated 176 citations; 35 (19.9%) were fabricated. Among the 141 real citations, 64 (45.4%) contained errors, most frequently incorrect or invalid digital object identifiers. Fabrication rates differed significantly by disorder (χ22=13.7; P=.001), with higher rates for binge eating disorder (17/60, 28%) and body dysmorphic disorder (14/48, 29%) than for major depressive disorder (4/68, 6%). While fabrication did not differ overall by review type, stratified analyses showed higher fabrication for specialized versus general reviews of binge eating disorder (11/24, 46% vs 6/36, 17%; P=.01). Accuracy rates also varied by disorder (χ22=11.6; P=.003), being lowest for body dysmorphic disorder (20/34, 59%) and highest for major depressive disorder (41/64, 64%). Accuracy rates differed by review type within some disorders, including higher accuracy for general reviews of major depressive disorder (26/34, 77% vs 15/30, 50%; P=.03). Conclusions Citation fabrication and bibliographic errors remain common in GPT-4o outputs, with nearly two-thirds of citations being fabricated or inaccurate. Reliability systematically varied by disorder familiarity and prompt specificity, with greater risks in less visible or specialized mental health topics. These findings highlight the need for careful prompt design, rigorous human verification of all model-generated references, and stronger journal and institutional safeguards to protect research integrity as LLMs are integrated into academic practice.

claims.text: GPT-4o generated fabricated citations at an overall rate of 19.9% across six mental health literature reviews.
Among non-fabricated citations generated by GPT-4o, 45.4% contained at least one bibliographic error.
Digital object identifiers (DOIs) were the most common bibliographic error type among real journal citations generated by GPT-4o.
Citation fabrication rates in GPT-4o outputs differed significantly across mental disorders based on research maturity and public visibility.
Specialized prompt reviews produced a significantly higher citation fabrication rate than general overview reviews for binge eating disorder.

limitations.text: The findings are based on three selected psychiatric conditions and may not generalize to other psychiatric disorders or specialized subfields.
Findings are specific to GPT-4o and may not generalize to outputs generated by other large language models.
The study evaluated standardized, straightforward prompts without implementing prompt engineering strategies such as retrieval-augmented or chain-of-thought prompting.
The evaluation analyzed a single generated output per prompt and did not assess intraprompt stochastic variability across multiple runs.

future_work.text: Assess whether similar patterns of citation fabrication and bibliographic errors occur across a broader range of mental health topics and other academic disciplines.
Investigate whether different large language models exhibit comparable citation fabrication patterns or model-specific reliability differences.
Test whether prompt engineering techniques like citation verification prompts reduce hallucination and citation error rates.
Examine multiple generations per prompt to evaluate the consistency and reproducibility of LLM-generated citations.
